title: Eat, drink, don't waste
hook: eat and drink but don't be wasteful (7:31)

segments.voice: Yesterday: libas, the garment, and the garment of piety. Your line was the best clothing is inside. Today, five verses later, from the closet to the kitchen.

Open almost any fridge on a Sunday night. Half a bag of spinach gone slimy. The rice nobody wanted. A yogurt two weeks past its date. Food that was paid for goes in the bin, and more gets bought. At the other end of the scale, a hadith shows the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ washing for prayer with about a double handful of water. Between those two pictures sits a short line in surah seven that sounds almost too simple to need saying.
screen: `THE SUNDAY NIGHT FRIDGE.` → `A DOUBLE HANDFUL OF WATER.` → `TOO SIMPLE TO NEED SAYING.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “O Children of Adam! Look to your adornment at every place of worship, and eat and drink, but be not prodigal. Lo! He loveth not the prodigals.” Two halves. The first is about clothing again. A report in Sahih Muslim explains why: before Islam, some people circled the Ka'bah unclothed, and this verse told them to come to worship dressed, even dressed well. The second half is about the table. Eat. Drink. Enjoy it; the next verse asks who could forbid the good things Allah has provided. But don't commit israf. The root s-r-f means to go past the limit, to overshoot: israf is excess, beyond what's needed. The Qur'an has a separate word, tabdhir, in surah seventeen, for scattering wealth away on nothing, and it's sharp about both. A hadith in Tirmidhi gives a measure for eating: a third of the stomach for food, a third for drink, a third for breath. And Bukhari records that the Prophet made wudu with a mudd, roughly what two cupped hands hold, and bathed with only a few times that. Teachers take it as a lesson: enough is a real amount, and you can find it. The verse doesn't say eat less than you need, or never enjoy food. It says eat, drink, and stop at enough. The opposite of israf isn't hunger. It's the right amount, used well.
screen: `DRESSED FOR WORSHIP.` · `EAT AND DRINK — ENJOY IT.` · `ISRAF — PAST THE LIMIT.` · `A THIRD, A THIRD, A THIRD.` · then, large: `BE NOT PRODIGAL.`

segments.voice: Walk through the day ahead in your mind and look, without judging, for the leaks: water running while you brush your teeth, food that will go bad, a light on in an empty room, a purchase you don't need. Then picture your next meal, eaten slowly, ending at enough, with a little room left for breath.
Israf. Excess, going past the limit. Surah seven: eat and drink, but don't be wasteful, for Allah does not love the wasteful. Today's word.
Your line: enough, no waste. The good things are a gift to enjoy. Day four hundred seven.

howItsDone: Muslims are taught to avoid israf in food, water and money; some keep the hadith of thirds in mind at meals, and teachers often point to the small amount of water the Prophet used for wudu.

what it means: enjoy what's provided, dressed with dignity, and stop at enough in food, drink and everything else.
what a scholar hears: israf (excess in quantity) and tabdhir (spending on what has no right) are distinct terms; Muslim 3028 gives the occasion of 7:31 as unclothed circling of the Ka'bah.

chat.meaning: Eat and drink, but be not prodigal (7:31). Israf means going past the limit; its opposite isn't hunger but the right amount.
